g) Issue a writ in the nature of Mandamus or any other
appropriate  Writ,  Order  or  grant  an  ad-interim
injunction restraining and prohibiting the Respondent
Bank,  its  agents,  servants,  and  privies  from
proceeding any further in pursuance of the actions
initiated under the SARFAESl Act, the RDB Act, or any
other law in force;
h) Pass any other orders which the Hon'ble Court deems
fit owing to the nature of circumstances.”
Learned counsel Shri Nedumpara pointed out that when once
there is a decree passed (ex-parte decree in the instant
case), namely O.A. No.439/2014 by the DRT, Ernakulam, the
principle of transit in rem judicatam  applies.  Further, the
general principle of res judicata applies and therefore, there
cannot be any further proceeding which can be taken as the
cause of action would have merged in the decree. He therefore,
contended  that  the  provision  of  the  Securitisation  and
Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security
Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act, 2002) could not have been
applied in the facts and circumstances of this case.
4

--- Page 437 ---
We have considered the said arguments advanced by Shri
Nedumpara.
We only refer to Section 35 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002,
which reads as under -
“35. The provisions of this Act to override other laws.- 
The  provisions  of  this  Act  shall  have  effect,  
notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained
in any other law for the time being in force or any 
instrument having effect by virtue of any such law.”
Having regard to the fact that the provisions of the
SARFAESI Act, 2002 have an overriding effect notwithstanding
anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for
the time being in force or any instrument having effect by
virtue of any other law, we find that the provisions of the
said Act would override.  Therefore, the contentions of
learned counsel Shri Nedumpara cannot be accepted.
Hence, the Writ Petition is dismissed.
Pending application(s) shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 82 OF 2025
ECOLOGIC CIRCLE LIMITED           PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
ECOSURE PULPMOLDING TECHNOLOGIES 
LIMITED RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 1996 (1996 Act), seeks the appointment of a sole
arbitrator to adjudicate disputes arising out of an Equipment Sales
Contract  and  an  Equipment  Installation  Contract,  both  dated
13.01.2025  (Contracts).  The  Contracts  concern  the  supply,
installation and commissioning of pulp-moulding equipment for the
Petitioner's project in Thailand.
2. Briefly stated, the Petitioner is a company incorporated under
the  laws  of  Thailand,  while  the  Respondent  is  a  company
incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 and existing under the
laws of India. Under the Contracts, the Respondent agreed to
supply, install and commission pulp-moulding machinery and allied
equipment for the Petitioner's project, together with associated
services. Clause 15 of the Equipment Sales Contract provides that
disputes arising out of or in connection with that contract shall
be finally settled by arbitration. Clause 16(b) of the Equipment
Installation Contract provides that, if negotiations fail, disputes
shall  be  referred  to  arbitration  under  the  Rules  of  the
1

--- Page 469 ---
International Chamber of Commerce. Clause 22 of that Contract also
contemplates  resolution  through  negotiation,  mediation  and
arbitration.
3. According to the Petitioner, it remitted USD 204,642 under the
Contracts. The Respondent, however, failed to manufacture, ship and
install the equipment within the agreed timelines or refund the
amount received. The Petitioner relies on subsequent communications
to  contend  that  the  Respondent  acknowledged  difficulties  in
performance, proposed cancellation of the Contracts and agreed to
refund the amount in instalments, but failed to do so. It is
further alleged that the Respondent thereafter caused a criminal
complaint to be filed before a court at Gautam Budh Nagar.
4. The Petitioner consequently invoked arbitration by notice
dated 11.10.2025 and proposed the appointment of a former Judge of
the High Court of Delhi as the sole arbitrator. The notice was sent
to the Respondent by email as well as by post and courier. The
Respondent did not reply. The Petitioner has therefore instituted
the present petition.
5. Since the Petitioner is incorporated in Thailand, the proposed
arbitration is an “international commercial arbitration” within the
meaning of Section 2(1)(f) of the 1996 Act. This Court, therefore,
has jurisdiction under Section 11(12)(a) of the 1996 Act.
6. Notice in these proceedings was delivered at the Respondent's
2

--- Page 470 ---
Greater Noida address. By order dated 26.05.2026, the Petitioner
was also directed to serve the Respondent through the learned
counsel appearing for it in certain other proceedings. Proof of
such service by email has been placed on record. Despite service,
no one has entered appearance for the Respondent.
7. We have heard learned Senior Counsel for the Petitioner and
perused the material on record. At the present stage of limited
scrutiny under Section 11, we are satisfied, prima facie, as to the
existence of an arbitration agreement and disputes falling within
its ambit.
8. Having regard to the facts and circumstances set out above, we
allow  the  Arbitration  Petition  and  appoint  Mr.  Rajiv  Jain,
Advocate, as the sole arbitrator to adjudicate the disputes arising
out of or in connection with the Contracts.
9. The appointment shall be subject to the learned Arbitrator
furnishing the disclosure contemplated under Section 12(1) of the
1996 Act and not being ineligible under Section 12(5) thereof.
10. All questions concerning the jurisdiction of the arbitral
tribunal, arbitrability, limitation, maintainability, and the scope
and interpretation of the arbitration clauses are left open to be
raised before the learned Arbitrator. It is clarified that we have
not  made  any  observation  on  the  merits  of  the  subsisting
dispute(s).
3

--- Page 471 ---
11. Notably, the Contracts do not expressly designate the seat of
arbitration. The Petitioner proposed New Delhi, India, in its
notice of invocation dated 11.10.2025, and the Respondent has not
appeared to object despite service. Accordingly, the seat and venue
of arbitration shall be New Delhi, India.
12. The  learned  Arbitrator  shall  be  at  liberty  to  fix  the
remuneration/fees in consultation with the parties. The Arbitration
Petition is allowed in the above terms. Ordered accordingly.
13. Pending  interlocutory  applications,  if  any,  also  stand

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal impugns an interim order dated 05.03.2024
whereby the Division Bench of the High Court, though
admitted the writ appeal, declined the prayer for stay
of the order impugned in the writ appeal.
4. The submission on behalf of the appellants is that if
the impugned order passed by the learned Single Judge is
allowed  to  operate,  they  would  suffer  serious
consequences as their appointments, which stood for
about nine years, would be jeopardized.
5. Upon  consideration  of  the  aforesaid  submission,  on
01.04.2024, while issuing notice in this appeal, an
interim order directing parties to maintain status quo
was passed.
6. Admittedly, the writ appeal is still pending before the
High Court. In such circumstances, in our view, ends of
justice would be best served if this appeal is disposed

--- Page 502 ---
of  by  directing  that  status  quo  as  on  date  qua
appointments shall be maintained till the disposal of
the writ appeal by the High Court.  
7. Accordingly, this appeal is disposed of by directing
that status quo  as on date shall be maintained pending
consideration of L.P.A. No. 38/2024 by the Division
Bench of the High Court.
8. We also request the High Court to ensure that the writ
appeal (L.P.A. No. 38/2024) along with other connected
appeals are decided preferably within a period of six
months from the date a certified copy of this order
placed before the High Court.
9. We make it clear that the interim protection accorded by
this Court shall not be a ground for the appellants to
claim any benefit on equity before the High Court.
10. The appeal as well as all pending applications are
disposed of in the aforesaid terms.

MOHIT SHARMA ..... APPELLANT(S)

STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, Mohit Sharma, is aggrieved by the order dated
31.03.2026 passed by a learned Judge of the High Court of
Judicature at Allahabad in Application u/s 529 BNSS No.
206/2026.  The said application was filed by respondent No. 2
herein, viz. the wife of the appellant, seeking expeditious
conclusion of the trial in Criminal Case No. 220/2021, titled
“State of U.P. vs. Mohit & Ors.” .  However, dealing with the
said application, the learned Judge deemed it appropriate to
direct the appellant to take his wife back, vide order dated
11.02.2026.
3. Thereafter, when respondent No. 2 reported to the Court that
the appellant had not complied with the said order dated
11.02.2026, the learned Judge passed the impugned order dated
31.03.2026, whereby he directed the arrest of the appellant
1

--- Page 530 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP(Crl.) No. 6167/2026
and his production before the Court on the next date, that
is, 09.04.2026.  
4. By order dated 08.04.2026, this Court stayed the operation of
the impugned order dated 31.03.2026.
5. We find that this is a fit case for interference, as the High
Court  was  not  justified  in  enlarging  the  scope  of  the
application filed by respondent No. 2, which merely sought
expeditious conclusion of a pending trial.  It was not for
the  High  Court  to  undertake  forcible  mediation  efforts
against the appellant under threat of arrest.
6. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed,  setting  aside  the
impugned order dated 31.03.2026.  Application under Section
529 BNSS No. 206/2026 shall stand restored to the file of the
High Court for consideration afresh on its own merits and in
accordance with law.
Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

I.A. NO.254002/2026 in SLP(Crl) No.7962/2026:
We  have  heard  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General (ASG) appearing for the respondent,  as
well as the learned Senior counsel appearing for
the applicant/petitioner.
The applicant/petitioner seeks interim bail on
the ground that his brother is likely to undergo
an eye surgery, and also that his minor child and
mother,  both  of  whom  suffer health  issues,
require his presence.
Learned A.S.G. appearing for the respondent,
while vehemently opposing the grant of interim
bail, submits that the disability of the said
child  is  long-standing, the  mother  does  not
require  any urgent medical treatment and the
2

--- Page 547 ---
brother is not living in the same household. 
Having considered the submissions, the fact
remains that the minor child of the petitioner
has been suffering from a hearing disability for
quite some time as a result of which he had to
undergo  a  bilateral  cochlear  implantation
surgery. 
De hors  the  submissions  that  the
applicant/petitioner wants to be with his minor
child and mother, t he further fact that the
brother of the applicant/petitioner is likely to
undergo an eye surgery, is not in dispute. In
addition to that, we have taken note of the fact
that  the  applicant/petitioner has  been  under
incarceration for a period of five years and
eleven months.
Hence, in  the facts and circumstances of the
case, we are inclined to grant interim bail to
the applicant/petitioner for a period of ten (10)
days, commencing from 11.09.2026 to 21.09.2026.
Accordingly,  the  applicant/petitioner  is
granted  interim  bail  from  11.09.2026  to
21.09.2026, subject to the terms and conditions
as may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court.
The applicant/petitioner shall surrender to the
concerned jail authorities on or before 5.00 PM
on 21.09.2026.

police escort  at  the  cost  of  the

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.     OF 2026
(arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.5494/2026
RAMESH                                             Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
MALLIKSAB                                          Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Mr. Manjunath Meled, learned counsel appearing for the respondent and
vehemently for the prayer being granted in favour of the appellant.
4. The appellant, who was the accused in the proceedings initiated under
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act filed by the respondent is before
this Court calling in question the judgment dated 11.09.2025 whereby the High
Court allowed the appeal and reversed the Trial Court judgment dated
15.04.2023 whereunder the appellant had been acquitted and has now been
convicted by the High Court imposing a fine of Rs. 3,00,000/- (Rs. Three Lakhs
only) with Rs. 2,90,000/- (Rs. Two Lakh Ninety Thousand only) to be paid to the
complainant as compensation and in default Simple Imprisonment of eight
months has been ordered.
5. The dispute arose from alleged hand loan of Rs. 1,60,000/- (Rs. One Lakh
Sixty Thousand only) borrowed by the accused for repayment of the same
cheque issued in favour of the respondent-complainant when presented came
to  be dishonored  and as  such the respondent-complainant  ignited  the

--- Page 554 ---
2
proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act. The Trial Court
on appreciation of the evidence held that the statutory presumption stood
rebutted on preponderance and probabilities, whereas the High Court while
reversing the said finding opined with the defense raised by the accused was
inconsistent and had not been probable.
6. Though, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner has raised several
contentions and urged various grounds to assail the impugned judgment, the
thrust of the argument or in other words the prime contention has been that
learned counsel for the appellant-accused before the High Court was absent on
the date of hearing and as such the High Court could not have disposed of the
appeal on merits without appointing an Amicus.
7. This Court time and again it has been held in various judgments that in
criminal matters, it would be incumbent upon the Court to appoint an Amicus
Curiae in case of learned counsel for the accused being absent. This proportion
has been reiterated in “Mohd Sukur Ali vs. State of Assam”  [AIR 2011 SC
1222].
8. Yet the High Court seems to have been swayed by the fact that the
counsel had been consistently not appearing and had not been assisting the
Court in conducting the proceedings, to reverse the findings of the Trial Court.
9. On the short ground that High Court not having appointed an Amicus
Curiae on behalf of the accused-appellant and there being not effective
representation of the accused or in other words, the accused having been
deprived of effective defense before the High Court, the impugned order would
not stand and as such it is hereby set aside. The matter stands remitted to the
jurisdictional High Court for being heard and disposed of on merits and in
accordance with law. It is made clear that we have not expressed any opinion

--- Page 555 ---
3
with regard to the merits and all contentions of the parties are kept open.
10. It is also made clear that both parties shall appear before the jurisdictional
High Court on 28.09.2026 with waiting for any further notice and in the event of
appellant-accused remaining absent on the said date or being unrepresented,
the jurisdictional High Court would be at liberty to appoint an Amicus Curiae or
appoint a counsel from the panel of Advocates of High Legal Services
Committee to conduct the proceedings and hear the appeal.
11. Learned counsel appearing for both the parties shall cooperate with the
High Court in expeditiously disposing of the matter.
12. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No.12202 of 2026)
SHER SINGH   APPELLANT
VERSUS
GOVT OF NCT OF DELHI & ORS.     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The only point raised in this appeal is
about the appellant’s entitlement to interest at
GPF  rate  on  the  amount  of  leave  encashment
released in his favor. Appellant’s O.A. No. 388
of  2023  was  allowed  with  the  following
directions:
“In view of the aforesaid, the impugned
orders dated 02.01.2019, 13.07.2020 and
29.09.2020 are quashed and set aside.
The  OA  stands  disposed  of  with  a
direction to the Competent Authority
amongst the respondents, who may pass
an appropriate order for release of the
leave  encashment  in  accordance  with
law. This exercise shall be completed
within a period of two months from the
date of receipt of copy of this Order.
There shall be no order as to costs.”
1

--- Page 562 ---
3. Being aggrieved by the above order, the
appellant moved the High Court by filing a Writ
Petition seeking interest for the delayed payment
of leave encashment amount on the ground that
Constable Anil Kumar, who was also dismissed from
service along with the appellant, has been paid
such interest at GPF rate.
4. It was also submitted that Anil Kumar had
also preferred O.A. No. 2709/2021, in which vide
order dated 18.04.2023, he was allowed interest
at the GPF rate, but such relief has not been
granted to the appellant.
5. The High Court has rejected the appellant’s
prayer for grant of interest at GPF rate and
instead has allowed interest @ 6% per annum. In
the  course  of  hearing  today,  the  appellant
appearing in-person has relied upon an order
passed by this Court in Jagdish  Prasad  Saini  &
Ors.  vs.  State  of  Rajasthan  &  Ors. , seeking
interest  @  10%  per  annum  from  the  date  of
entitlement to the leave encashment.
6. Having heard the parties, we find that the
appellant’s basic case before the Tribunal was
for seeking interest at the GPF rate as has been
allowed  in  favor  of  Constable  Anil  Kumar.
Therefore, the appellant cannot improve his case
2

--- Page 563 ---
merely because in some other judgment this Court
has allowed interest @ 10% per annum in the facts
of the said case (Jagdish Prasad Saini's case).
7. In our considered view, the appellant is
indeed entitled to interest at GPF rate as was
prevailing on the date when such benefit has been
allowed in favor of Constable Anil Kumar by order
passed in June 2024 (annexed as Annexure P-2 to
the SLP).
8. In view of the above, the Civil Appeal is
allowed in-part and it is directed that the
appellant  shall  be  entitled  to  interest  on
delayed payment of leave encashment at the GPF
rate at the same rate which has been granted to
Constable Anil Kumar.
9. No order as to costs.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

    ………………………………………………………J.

21(c)  and  29  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and
Psychotropic Substances, 1985.
3. We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing for the appellant and the learned
counsel appearing for the respondent.
4. This is the third round of litigation. On the
last occasion, we have clearly indicated that in
the  event  of  trial  is  not  proceeding
1 SLP(Crl.) No.12651/2026

--- Page 566 ---
sufficiently, the appellant was given liberty to
approach this Court, pursuant to which, he has
filed the present appeal. 
5. Taking note of the above fact that the trial is
not proceeding, coupled with the submissions
made by the learned Senior counsel appearing for
the  appellant,  that  he  has  been  under
incarceration for a period of two and a half
years, we are inclined to set aside the impugned
order  passed  by  the  High  Court,  and  grant
regular bail to the appellant.

aside, and the appellant is granted regular
bail, subject to the terms and conditions that
may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court.
7. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.                 OF 2026  
@ SLP (CRL.) NO.15748/2026
ANKIT RATHI & ANR. APPELLANTS
                              VERSUS
STATE OF NCT OF DELHI & ANR.      RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellants, who have been visited with a summons in Crl.M.C.
No.3675/2019, challenged the same before the jurisdictional High Court
and by order dated 30.07.2019, notice was issued by the High Court and
the proceedings before the trial court was stayed.
4. Subsequently, respondent No.2 – complainant has appeared and
contested  the  matter.  Though  it  is  contended  that  the  appellants
(accused  persons)  have  taken  adjournments,  we  are  not  going  to
examine the said contentions as the records would speak itself.
5. Be that as it may, when the matter was listed for hearing on
30.07.2026, Mr. Chandra Shekhar Yadav, learned counsel appearing for
the appellants before the High Court had not appeared and a request for
adjournment was made on his behalf and by the impugned order, the
1

--- Page 570 ---
said request was rejected after taking note of the fact that after several
years, the matter was listed for hearing and yet the learned counsel was
not ready and willing to proceed with the matter. However, it is the
contention of the learned counsel appearing for the appellants before
this  Court  that  counsel  for  the  appellant  was  engaged  before  the
National Company Law Tribunal Allahabad Bench at Prayagraj and was
on his legs on the said date, i.e., on 30.07.2026. To evidence this fact,
the record of proceedings of NCLT dated 02.07.2026 and 30.07.2026 has
been placed on record including the boarding pass reflecting that the
learned counsel had traveled from Delhi to Prayagraj on the previous
day of hearing, i.e., on 29.07.2026. Hence, he could not appear before
the High Court of Delhi.
6. The party appearing in person – respondent No.2 has vehemently
opposed by contending that appellants are using all dilatory tactics to
protract the proceedings and because of this reason, the High Court had
rightly vacated the interim order of stay on 30.07.2026 and as such he
prays for the confirmation of the said order.
7. Though no fault can be laid at the doors of the High Court, yet we
feel that one accommodation could have been extended to the appellant
herein and rightly so the High Court had adjourned the matter which in
fact means the request for adjournment was acceded to. However, the
High Court in the same breath seems to have vacated the interim order
which was in operation for seven years and the very purpose of filing the
2

--- Page 571 ---
quashing petition would get defeated if stay of proceedings before trial
court is vacated. Hence, we are of the considered view that said order
requires to be set aside and the order of stay which was granted on
30.07.2019 which was in operation till it was vacated on 30.07.2006
should continue till the disposal of the proceedings. Since, seven years
have lapsed, the complainant – respondent No.2 cannot be made to
suffer. We request the High Court to take up for hearing the pending
proceedings expeditiously and preferably on or before 10.10.2026 for
which the learned counsel appearing for the appellants also agree and
consents. He also assures the Court that as and when the matter is
listed before the Court, he would address the arguments. Placing his
submission and undertaking on record, we request the High Court to
dispose of the matter expeditiously and after preponing the matter to
any date convenient to the Court and matter be taken up for hearing
preferably on or before 10.10.2026. With these observations, the appeal
is allowed and the impugned order is set aside.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal  No(s).  /2026
      @SLP (Crl) No. 13531/2026
BUTA KHAN @ BAGGA KHAN                             Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF PUNJAB                                    Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order  dated
02.07.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and
Haryana at Chandigarh rejecting the prayer of the
appellant for suspension of sentence awarded by the
trial court.
4. The  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant
submits that sentence awarded for conviction under
Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1973 is five
years  and  by  now  he  has  already  suffered
incarceration of about three years. Besides, it has
been submitted that the injury has been found to be
on a non vital part, simple in nature.
5. Having regard to the above, by taking into
1

--- Page 594 ---
consideration that the appeal is not likely to be
heard in near future, we are of the view that the
High Court ought to have suspended the sentence
pending consideration of the appeal.
6. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed and the
order of the High Court rejecting the prayer of the
appellant for suspension of sentence is set aside.
The sentence awarded by the trial court shall
remain  suspended  pending  consideration  of  the
appeal.
7. The appellant shall be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the trial court may
deem fit to impose in the facts and circumstances
of the case.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

--- Page 599 ---
2. Learned Attorney General for India informs that, in view of
Section 24(1)(d) of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 (in short,
‘2026 Act’), 248 members of different Tribunals have been found
eligible for extension, including those whose term was extended
till today. He further informed that such members will get an
automatic extension subject to the condition of completing the
maximum tenure of five years or attaining the age of 70 years or 67
years, as the case may be.
3. We have also heard the parties with respect to the issue of
two judicial members and one expert member of the National Green
Tribunal (NGT), whose extended term is expiring today. Though these
members may not be entitled to seek further extension in view of
the age embargo, the learned Attorney General states that the
selection process for appointment of new members will be completed
very soon. 
4. Keeping the aforesaid in mind and in order to ensure that the
day-to-day functioning of the NGT is not hampered, as an interim
measure, we direct that the two judicial members and one expert
member shall continue till fresh appointments are made in their
place. 
5. Similar  reports  have  been  received  in  respect  of  other
Tribunals  also,  where  the  judicial/technical/expert/
administrative, etc. members are required to be appointed by the
Central Government. 
6. It goes without saying that the Union of India shall take up
the matter of fresh appointments in accordance with the provisions
3

--- Page 600 ---
of the 2026 Act without any delay.
7. In view of the above observation, Miscellaneous Applications
bearing  Diary  Nos.  11555/2026,  53087/2026  as  well  as  I.A.
No.105911/2026 in SLP(C) Nos.11021-11022/2020 are disposed of.
Pending applications, if any, shall also stand closed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner is an accused in the proceedings arising out of
ECIR/RPZO/09/2022 dated 29.09.2022, registered by the Enforcement
Directorate (ED) under Sections 3 and 4 of the Prevention of Money
Laundering Act, 2002. 
2. The predicate case originated from FIR No.129/2022 dated
12.07.2022, registered at Bengaluru under Sections 186, 204, 353
and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
3. The petitioner is the promoter of M/s Indermani Group and is
alleged to have assisted the principal accused in money laundering
by  purchasing  benami properties  to  safeguard  the  ill-gotten
proceeds of crime. The petitioner was arrested by ED on 13.10.2022.
Subsequently,  he  was  granted  interim  bail  by  this  Court  on
17.05.2024, which was made absolute on 07.08.2024.
4. During the pendency of the trial, the petitioner sought
permission  to  travel  to  Abu  Dhabi,  UAE,  for  specialized
physiotherapy at Khan Kinetic Treatment, Orthopedic Spine Center,
Abu Dhabi. However, the said request was declined by the Special
Court as well as the Chhattisgarh High Court, prompting the
petitioner to approach this Court.
5. Mr. Gopal Sankaranarayanan, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the petitioner, submits that the petitioner is required to
travel to Abu Dhabi, UAE, for the specialized treatment, which will
be carried out in four different spells, each comprising one week.
It is further submitted that the petitioner shall return to India
2

--- Page 611 ---
upon completion of each such spell. 
6. In  the  peculiar  facts  and  circumstances,  we  allow  the
petitioner to travel to Abu Dhabi, UAE, for his treatment at Khan
Kinetic Treatment, Orthopedic Spine Center, Abu Dhabi, subject to
the following conditions:
(i) The petitioner shall, before undertaking the first visit to Abu
Dhabi, file an affidavit with the Registry of this Court setting
out  the  specific  details  of  each  of  the  four  spells,  each
comprising one week. 
(ii) Upon returning to India after each spell, the petitioner shall
inform the concerned local office of the ED of his return.
(iii)The petitioner shall return to India on or before the date
stipulated for each visit.
(iv) The petitioner shall continue to abide by the terms and
conditions imposed while granting bail.
(v) The petitioner is restrained from opening or closing any bank
account  outside  India  and/or  from  undertaking  any  property
transaction abroad during the period of his stay.
(vi) The  petitioner  shall  not  directly  or  indirectly  delay,
obstruct or frustrate the pending proceedings before the Special
Court (PMLA), Raipur.
(vii) The petitioner will also appear before ED as and when
summoned after his return.
3

--- Page 612 ---
(viii) The petitioner shall deposit a sum of Rs. 1 crore as
refundable security with the Registry of this Court at least one
week prior to his departure.
7. Post the matter on 30.10.2026 for ensuring compliance.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO.43 OF 2025
BEST ORGANIC INGREDIENTS PTY.
LTD. PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
EXPOVAN & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(5) of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 1996 (Act) seeks the appointment of a sole
arbitrator to adjudicate disputes arising from a Memorandum of
Understanding dated 26.05.2024, executed between the Petitioner(s)
and the Respondent(s).
2. Briefly observed, the Petitioner, Best Organic Ingredients
Pty. Ltd., is an Australian entity engaged in the business of trade
and supply of various organic food products, including vanilla
beans.  Respondent  No.  1,  Expovan,  is  a  partnership  firm
incorporated in India. Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are partners in the
Respondent No. 1-firm, while Respondent No. 4 is the firm’s Head of
Business Development. The Petitioner company, on various occasions,
sold vanilla beans to the Respondent No. 1-firm.
3. It is alleged that Respondent No. 1 began defaulting on
payments due to the Petitioner from July 2020. After various
communications and complaints, the parties arrived at a settlement
recorded in a Memorandum of Understanding dated 26.05.2024, under
which Respondent No. 1 acknowledged an outstanding amount of USD
1

--- Page 614 ---
500,000 and committed to clearing the same through staggered
payments by the third week of June 2024. Clause 7 of the Memorandum
provides that disputes not resolved through mutual discussion shall
be referred to arbitration, with the seat in India and the language
of arbitration being English.
4. It is further contended that Respondent No. 1 has again failed
to make its payments in terms of the Memorandum of Understanding.
It appears that the attempts to amicably settle the disputes
through mutual discussion between the parties also failed. In these
circumstances,  the  Petitioner  sought  to  initiate  arbitral
proceedings and issued an arbitration notice dated 20.12.2024. It
suggested  the  name  of  Mr.  Ashish  Batra,  Advocate,  as  the
arbitrator. However, the Respondent has not responded to the
notice. Hence, the Petitioner has filed the instant Petition,
seeking appointment of a sole arbitrator.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
material placed on record.
6. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances recorded above and
the relevant provision under the Memorandum of Understanding dated
24.05.2024, we deem it just and proper to allow the instant
Arbitration Petition and appoint Justice R Suresh Kumar, former
Judge, Madras High Court as the Sole Arbitrator to resolve the
disputes between the parties. Keeping in view the facts and
circumstances of this case, the seat and venue of arbitration shall
be Chennai, India.
2

--- Page 615 ---
7. The  Arbitrator  shall  have  the  liberty  to  fix  his  own
remuneration/fees. Ordered accordingly.
8. Pending  interlocutory  applications,  if  any,  also  stand
disposed of.

..........................J.
       (JOYMALYA BAGCHI)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
 CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 729-730/2013
KAMALAWWA PARASANAGOUDA PATIL 
(DEAD) THROUGH LRS. & ORS.  APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
RENAWWA (DEAD) THROUGH LRS. & ORS.                RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Appellants lay challenge to the judgment and order dated
05/07/2011 in RFA No.1362/2004 titled “Rajakumar Vs.Renawwa &
Ors. and RFA No.113/2005 titled “Kamalawwa Parasanagouda Patil &
Ors. vs. Renawwa & Ors.” passed by the High Court of Karnataka
Circuit Bench at Dharwad.
2. Having heard learned counsel for the parties at length, we
are of the considered view that no case for interference is made
out in the present appeals.  The issue before the High Court
pertained to the paternity of original defendant No.5.  It reads
as under:
    “5. Whether def-5 proves that he is the son born
    to deceased Parasanagouda Patil and is entitled to 
    his legitimate share over the suit properties?”
3. The said issue was decided in the negative, against the
plaintiff.  Resultantly, the aggrieved party preferred an appeal
before the High Court.  Based on the submissions made by the
1

--- Page 622 ---
parties, the High Court inter  alia framed the following points
for consideration for itself:
“(i) Whether the finding recorded by Trial Court
that 5th defendant has failed to establish that
he is not the son of Parasanagouda Patil call
           for any interference?
(ii) What is the legitimate share to which the
  parties to the suit are entitled to on the death
           of deceased Parasanagouda Patil?”
4.  In answering the same, the High Court referred to the
evidence led by the parties (ocular and documentary). We notice
that the High Court has reversed the findings of fact returned
by the Trial Court.  The High Court has answered the  point for
consideration in favour of the appellant i.e original defendant
No.5, holding him to be the son of Parasanagouda Patil.  Such
findings of fact, apart from ocular evidence, are based on the
unrefuted documentary evidence i.e.(i) Voters List; (ii) School
Transfer Certificate; and (iii)the admission made by the parties
in collateral proceedings.
5. We are of the considered view that the findings of fact
returned by the High Court cannot be said to be perverse or
erroneous in any manner.
6. In our considered view, the High Court rightly overturned
findings of fact as returned by the Trial Court.
7. In this view of the matter, we see no reason to interfere
with the impugned judgment and order dated 05/07/2011 in RFA
2

--- Page 623 ---
No.1362/2004  titled  “Rajakumar  Vs.  Renawwa  &  Ors.  and  RFA
No.113/2005 titled “Kamalawwa Parasanagouda Patil & Ors. vs.
Renawwa & Ors.” passed by the High Court of Karnataka Circuit
Bench at Dharwad.
8. Accordingly, the appeals stand dismissed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

2026 passed by the High Court of  Himachal Pradesh at

the High Curt has rejected the bail application of the
petitioner in connection with FIR No. 120 of 2025 dated
19th August, 2025 registered at Police Station Dhalli,
District Shimla, Himachal Pradesh for offences punishable
under Sections 21 and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short, “the NDPS
Act”).

submits that the petitioner has already undergone 1 year
in custody and the co-accused/Gurpreet Singh was also
travelling in the car has also been enlarged on bail.
4. Learned counsel for the respondent-State vehemently

the petitioner has a criminal antecedent while the co-
accused/Gurpreet Singh did not.  Learned counsel has also
drawn our attention to the status report filed which
indicates that the petitioner was addicted to the drug in
question.

that pertains to a case of Section 379 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860.
         SLP (Criminal) No.9079/2026                                                              Page 2 of 3

--- Page 648 ---
6. Having  considered  the  overall  facts  and
circumstances,  the  period  of  incarceration  already
undergone and the fact that the trial is expected to take
some time to conclude and keeping in mind the dictum of
Article 21 of the Constitution of India as well as the
twin-conditions in Section 37 of the NDPS Act, we direct
that pending trial, the petitioner shall be enlarged on
bail subject to the satisfaction of the Trial Court.  We
have also kept in mind the co-accused/Gurpreet Singh has

Mr. Kaustubh Chaturvedi, Adv.
              
1

--- Page 713 ---
Diary No.46970/2026
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. A recruitment carried out in haste in 2021-22 to the post of
Assistant Professors/Lecturers in the State of Punjab was set
aside by this Court finding it to be in violation of UGC
regulations and avoiding the Public Service Commission; which
was a statutory mandate. The judgment was passed on 14.07.2025
and the State was directed to initiate recruitment process as
per the UGC Regulations of 2018, which is in force in the
State of Punjab. Till date nothing has been done is the
grievance raised in the Miscellaneous Application.
 
2. We heard Sri Preetesh Kapur, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the applicant, Sri P.S. Patwalia and Sri Ranjit Kumar,
learned Senior Counsel appearing for the selected candidates,
Sri  Shadan  Farasat,  learned  Additional  Advocate  General
appearing for the State.
3. Sri  Shadan  Farasat,  learned  Additional  Advocate  General,
confesses that the State has not been able to finalize the
recruitment process, more because of the identification of the
reservation post, which is taking some time. He undertakes
before us that it will be done in a time-bound manner and the
State will file an affidavit indicating the clear timelines.
4. Sri P.S. Patwalia and Sri Ranjit Kumar, appearing for the
2

--- Page 714 ---
Diary No.46970/2026
selected candidates, who are continuing, pending recruitment
submits that let the selections be carried out of the entire
vacancies now existing.
5. We are not inclined to issue such directions in the MA;
especially since the protection of candidates eligible as on
2021-22 can only apply to the vacancies that were advertised
earlier, which recruitment was set aside subsequently by this
Court. The State could definitely carry out simultaneous
recruitment but not by the very same notifications.
6. Considering the submissions made by the learned Additional
Advocate General for the State, we direct an appropriate
affidavit  to  be  placed  on  record  within  two  weeks,  in
accordance with our directions above.
7. We remind the State that the candidates selected through
erroneous  recruitment  are  continuing,  and  we  make  this
concession only reckoning the plight of the students, whose
studies would be hampered otherwise.
8. We also caution the State that the concession need not put the
State into a slumber, since if clear timelines are not
provided, we would not hesitate to pass drastic orders.
9. List the matter on 30.09.2026.
  (CHANDRESH)                                     (POOJA SHARMA)
  ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)

Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. A suit of 2003 is kept pending on the ground of the learned
Single Judge before whom the suit is pending, having accepted the
written statement with long delay even without an application. We
find from the impugned order that the Division Bench of the High
Court noticed that the written statement was accepted only to
further the disposal of the suit, which had been pending since
2003. After two decades and three years, still the suit has not
proceeded an inch.
2. In the above circumstances, we affirm the order impugned
herein. Insofar as the written statement filed on record having
been accepted by the learned Single Judge, the suit shall be
proceeded with on its own merits. If a prayer is made for
expeditious disposal and the parties co-operate, the Court before
which the suit is pending, shall endeavour so to do.
3. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of.

Crl.A. @ SLP(Crl.) No. 9449/2026
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(arising out of SLP(Crl.) No. 9449/2026)
PREM SHANKAR DWIVEDI ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Challenge in this appeal is to the interim order dated
19.08.2010  passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Judicature  at
Allahabad in Criminal Revision No. 3325/2010.  By the said
order, the High Court stayed further proceedings in Sessions
Trial No. 296/2010, titled “ State vs. Ankit Pandey & Ors.”.
This was a case arising under Section 306 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860, and charges were framed therein by the Additional
Sessions Judge, F.T.C.-1, on 24.05.2010.
3. Aggrieved thereby, respondent No. 2 filed the aforestated
criminal revision before the High Court.  Despite the matter
having been kept pending for over a decade and a half, we are
informed that the same has not been taken up till date. In
the meanwhile, proceedings in the case stand frozen, owing to
the interim order passed by the High Court as long back as on
19.08.2010.  In effect, the trial stands stalled and the case
1

--- Page 764 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP(Crl.) No. 9449/2026
has not proceeded at all for over 16 years.
4. Having  deemed  it  appropriate  to  grant  stay  of  further
proceedings, the High Court ought to have taken adequate
measures to dispose of the case as expeditiously as possible.
Failing to do so and prolonging the stay for so long makes a
mockery of the criminal justice delivery system.  
5. Though this Court would ordinarily be disinclined to fix time
frames for disposal of cases by the High Courts, we find this
a fit case to make an exception and direct the High Court to
dispose of Criminal Revision No. 3325/2010 within six months
from today, failing which the interim order dated 19.08.2010
passed therein shall stand automatically vacated upon expiry
of the aforestated six month period.  It is for respondent
No. 2, who is the petitioner in the criminal revision, to
take necessary steps for expeditious hearing and disposal
thereof within the aforestated time frame.
6. The appeal is allowed in the aforesaid terms.
Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

cancellation of the bail by the High Court. We may, however, note
that the order cancelling the petitioner’s bail was passed by the
High Court on 04.05.2026 and this special leave petition was filed
on  30.05.2026.  Thereafter,  an  application  was  filed  seeking
condonation of the delay of 10 days in its refiling on 23.07.2026.
Had there been any urgency on the part of the petitioner, he
would have ensured that the matter was listed before this Court as
soon as possible to enable him to seek interim relief.  However, no
such steps were taken.  
The matter was listed before this Court only on 03.08.2026 and
notice was issued to the State of Gujarat.  No interim order was
passed on the said date by this Court.  
Today, when the matter is taken up, we are informed by the
learned counsel appearing for the State of Gujarat that the
petitioner failed to surrender after cancellation of the bail
granted to him and non-bailable warrants were issued against him on
21.08.2026 and 02.09.2026. 
The petitioner’s conduct in willfully choosing to ignore the
inevitable consequence that followed the impugned order dated
04.05.2026 cannot be overlooked. Having suffered the cancellation
of his bail he failed to take steps to secure interim relief in
that regard. The petitioner, therefore, ought to have surrendered
immediately or as soon as he could. His failure to do so till date
amounts to a clear abuse of process. This Court is not inclined to
show him any indulgence in these circumstances.
The special leave petition is, accordingly, dismissed on that
2

short ground.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION 
TRANSFER PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 3494 OF 2025 
 
SUN JOT SINGH 
PRITHVI PAL SINGH SOHAL             …PETITIONER 
 
VERSUS 
JASVINDER KAUR SAINI    …RESPONDENTS 
 
O R D E R 
1. The present petition has been filed by the petitioner-husband 
seeking transfer of HMA Petition No. 43 of 2025 instituted by 
the respondent -wife, from the Court of Principal Judge, 
Family Court, Paonta Sahib, District Sirmour , Himachal 
Pradesh to the Family Court Belapur, Navi Mumbai, 
Maharashtra.  
2. The marriage between the parties was solemnized on 
31.05.2022 as per Sikh rites and customs. The parties 
started residing in Mumbai at the residence of petitioner’s 
parents. The parties have been residing separately since June 
2024 
3. The respondent-wife filed Divorce Petition HMA No.43 of 2025 
under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (for short, 
the Act) for dissolution of marriage along with an application 
for interim maintenance  under Section 24 of the Act before 
the Family Court, Paonta Sahib. Aggrieved thereby, the 
petitioner-husband filed the present petition.  

--- Page 782 ---
T.P . (CIVIL) NO.3494/2025  2 
 
4. During the pendency of the present petition, this Court vide 
order dated 09.04.2026 referred the disputes to the Supreme 
Court Mediation Center to explore the possibility of 
settlement through mediation. Pursuant thereto, the parties 
have participated in the mediation proceedings and have 
entered into a Settlement Agreement dated 15.07.2026. We 
are informed that in furtherance of the settlement, the parties 
have resumed cohabitation 
5. We have examined the Settlement Agreement and have 
interacted with the parties. The parties have voluntarily 
agreed to make a sincere attempt to reconcile and rebuild 
their matrimonial relationship. The settlement records that 
the parties have resolved to resume their matrimonial 
relationship and have agreed to work together to resolve any 
differences that might arise in the future through mutual 
discussion and understanding.  
6. They have further agreed to end all litigation s pending 
between the parties. The Settlement Agreement also provides 
for return of the respondent -wife's stridhan and records the 
reciprocal rights, obligations and undertakings agreed upon 
by the parties for giving effect to the settlement.  
7. We are satisfied that the agreement has been entered into by 
the parties voluntarily and out of their own free will, without 
any force or coercion, in the presence of the learned Mediator 
and their respective counsel. In our considered view, the 
amicable resolution arrived at through mediation brings a 
quietus to all pending disputes.  Accordingly, the Settlement 
Agreement dated 15.07.2026 is accepted and shall form part 

--- Page 783 ---
T.P . (CIVIL) NO.3494/2025  3 
 
of this order. The parties shall remain bound by each of the 
terms and conditions incorporated therein. 
8. We direct that all pending cases between the parties shall 
stand quashed and closed. The amount deposited by the 
petitioner before the High Court of Himachal Pradesh shall 
also be released in his favour forthwith. 
9. We record our sincere appreciation for the efforts undertaken 
by the learned mediator Ms. Asha Gopalan Nair in facilitating 
an amicable settlement between the parties. We also record 
our appreciation for the support given and the positive 
approach taken by the parties and their respective counsel. 
10. The transfer petition stands disposed of in the aforesaid 
terms. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
Registry shall communicate this order to all the concerned 
Courts where the matters were pending and have been closed 
by this order. Formal orders may be passed by the respective 
Courts closing the proceedings. The Registry shall also draw 
the decree accordingly.

1. The petitioner challenges the rejection of his anticipatory bail
application by the High Court in connection with FIR No. 77 of 2025
registered at PS Sadar, District Chaibasa under Sections 376, 504,
506 and 509 of Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, “the IPC”).
2. The Petitioner is accused of establishing physical relationship with
the prosecutrix on the promise of marriage, and further threatening
to release their intimate videos.
3. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that it is not in
dispute that the parties were in a relationship since 17.09.2023 and
the FIR was filed by the prosecutrix only on 25.09.2025, after being
in a relationship with the Petitioner for over 2 years.
 
4. After considering the facts and circumstances of this case, we are
of the opinion that the material against the petitioner falls short
of the threshold required for refusal of anticipatory bail. 
5. Therefore, we order that in the event of arrest of the petitioner in
connection with the offence enumerated above, he shall be released
on bail, subject to terms and conditions that the Investigating
SLP(Crl.)  No. 3601/2026

Officer may deem fit to impose. He is also required to cooperate in
the investigation. 
6. Once the petitioner is released on bail by the IO, on directions
issued by the IO or summons issued by the jurisdictional court, the
petitioner shall appear before the jurisdictional court and furnish
fresh bail bonds and ensure due appearance in the trial.
7. With the aforesaid, this petition stands disposed of.
8. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner has been denied anticipatory bail by
the High Court  in connection with FIR No. 185 of 2025
registered at PS Beas Amritsar under Section 318(4) of
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023  and Section 13 of Punjab
Travel Professional Regulation Act, 2014.
2. The  Petitioner  is  alleged  to  have  cheated  the
complainant of Rs.1,43,500/- on the pretext of sending his
son to Dubai and securing a job for him. However, the
complainant’s son was sent to Dubai on a tourist visa
instead of a work visa, due to which, he had to come back
to India at his own expense.
3. High Court rejected the Petitioner’s anticipatory bail
application on the ground that the allegations make out a
prima  facie  case  for  cheating,  and  that  custodial
interrogation  is  required  for  conducting  proper
investigation in the matter.
4. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that
the Petitioner’s son knew that he was going on a tourist
visa  and  there  was  no  promise  of  job  made  by  the
Petitioner. There is also a civil suit between the parties,
SLP(Crl.)  No.6803/2026                                           2

--- Page 804 ---
and the complaint appears to be motivated. The Petitioner
does not have any criminal antecedents, much less any of a
similar kind.
5. After considering the facts and circumstances of this
case, we are of the opinion that the material against the
petitioner  falls  short  of  the  threshold  required  for
refusal of anticipatory bail. 
6. Therefore, we order that in the event of arrest of the
petitioner in connection with the offence enumerated above,
he  shall  be  released  on  bail,  subject  to  terms  and
conditions that the Investigating Officer may deem fit to
impose. He is also required to cooperate and submit the
evidentiary materials as required by the I.O. 
7. Once the petitioner is released on bail by the IO, on
directions issued by the IO or summons issued by the
jurisdictional court, the petitioner shall appear before
the jurisdictional court and furnish fresh bail bonds and
ensure due appearance in the trial.
8. With the aforesaid, this petition stands disposed of.
9. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

1. Pursuant to our Order dated 11.08.2026, the National Highways
Authority  of  India  has  given  a  proposal  to  the  landholders
regarding the compensation which they propose to pay. The proposal
letter dated 20.08.2026 has been placed before us.  It appears from

the land, and interest at the rate of 9% per annum on the enhanced

--- Page 810 ---
compensation, after deducting the amount previously released, from
the date of taking possession of the acquired land up to the date
of the order passed by the High Court. Further, they are agreeable
to consider payment of solatium.
2. Learned counsel for the landholders submits that the rate
appears to be on the lower side and further, the interest would
have to be paid not up to the date of the order passed by the High
Court but up to the date of the payment.  Further, the payment of
solatium  and  interest  thereupon  are  statutorily  mandated  and
therefore,  that  part  should  also  be  there  in  the  proposal.
Besides, there are other statutory benefits which have not been
spelt out in the offer.
3. In such circumstances, we deem it appropriate to require the
landholders to submit their concrete proposal before the Committee
appointed for fixing the compensation. The Committee shall consider
such counter proposal and take appropriate decision.
4. List these matters after six weeks.

O R D E R
1. Heard. Leave granted.
2.  The  present  appeal  is  directed  against  the  order  dated
03.06.2024 passed by the National Consumers Disputes Redressal
Commission, New Delhi (NCDRC) in First Appeal No.151/2013.
3. It is the contention of Mr.Atulesh Kumar, learned counsel
appearing for appellant that impugned judgment has been passed by a
single member (President) of the NCDRC. The coram itself being
incomplete, the matter ought to be remanded back for adjudication
afresh by setting aside the impugned order. He submits that
impugned judgment has also been questioned on merits and at this
juncture he would not intent to canvas the same, in the event of
this Court is inclined to remand the matter back to the NCDRC for
adjudication afresh.
4. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent-Insurance
Company would not dispute the fact that the impugned order has been
1

--- Page 815 ---
passed by a single member of the Commission but would submit that
such power is available to the President to pass such orders.
5. This Court under similar circumstances in catena of judgments,
namely, in Civil Appeal No.6569 of 2023 disposed of on 10.05.2024
and in Civil Appeal No.3953 of 2018 disposed of on 28.08.2024, has
consistently held that when the judgment is passed by a single
member of the tribunal, the coram itself is incomplete. In the
light of law laid down by this Court of which we are in agreement,
we are of the opinion that this matter ought to be remanded back to
the NCDRC for fresh decision. Hence, the impugned judgment dated
03.06.2024 is set aside and matter is remitted back to NCDRC for
being adjudicated afresh. No opinion is expressed on merits by the
same. Parties are directed to appear before the Registrar of NCDRC
on 24.09.2026 for a date to be fixed for arguments before the
Bench.
6. The appeal is allowed in the aforesaid terms by leaving the
parties to bear their own costs.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
INHERENT JURISDICTION
REVIEW PETITION (CRL) NO. 465 OF 2026 
IN
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL) NO. 11994 OF 2026
APOORV PRATAP SINGH & ORS.             PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR AND ANOTHER                 RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present Review Petition has been preferred against the Order dated
10.07.2026 passed by this Court in SLP (Crl.) No. 11994 of 2026, whereby the
Special Leave Petition filed against the judgment dated 10.03.2026 passed by the
High Court of Judicature at Patna (hereinafter referred to as “the High Court”)
in Criminal Appeal (SJ) No. 1853 of 2024 was dismissed.
2. By the judgment impugned in the aforesaid Special Leave Petition, the
High Court declined to quash the order dated 12.01.2023 passed by the
Additional District & Sessions Judge-I-cum-Special Judge, Kaimur at Bhabhua
(hereinafter referred to as “the trial Court”), whereby the application filed by the
petitioners seeking discharge was rejected.  
3. We have perused the material placed on record. 
1

--- Page 881 ---
4. It appears that the petitioners had sought discharge, which application
came to be dismissed by the trial Court, observing that at the stage of framing of
charge, the Court is required to examine the material on record only for the
limited purpose of determining whether a prima facie  case is made out against
the accused. The challenge to the said order was also dismissed by the High
Court.
5. Upon consideration of the material placed before it, this Court found no
ground to interfere with the impugned judgment and accordingly dismissed the
Special Leave Petition.

substantially the same as those urged earlier and do not disclose any error
apparent on the face of the record or any other ground warranting review. No
case for review is, therefore, made out by the petitioners. 
7. Accordingly, the present Review Petition is dismissed.

imprisonment of around 17 years and 14 days with remission. Co-accused Nos.
7-(Ajay Kumar) and 2 (Vijay Kumar) against whom similar allegations had been

Court by Order dated 18.05.2026 has granted bail to them. Appellant is
standing on the same footing and would also be entitled for suspension of
2

sentence and grant of bail on the ground of parity.

and being similarly placed and co-accused having been granted bail, on the
ground of parity the application deserves to be allowed. Accordingly, the
Interlocutory Application No. 207600/2026 seeking for grant of bail is allowed
and sentence imposed on the appellant is suspended and appellant is ordered
to be released on bail on such terms and conditions as the trial Court may deem
fit to impose. Records have been received.

3. Heard learned counsel for the petitioner and the respondents.
We do not need to dwell deep into the facts as the orders impugned
are interim in nature, intending to protect the interests of both
the parties pending disposal of the petition under Section 34 of
the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
4. Out of the Principal amount of Rs. 6.6 crores with 15%
interest, the Judgment Debtor, being the petitioner and Arunanchal
Power Development Agency [APDA] have cumulatively deposited a total
amount of Rs. 5.46 crores as of today.  We are of the opinion that
the amount already deposited is sufficient to protect the interests
of all the parties pending disposal of the Section 34 petition.  
5. In view of the above modification of the order passed by the
High Court, we direct that no further amounts need to be deposited
by the petitioner or Arunanchal Power Development Agency as an
interim  measure  till  the  petition  under  Section  34  of  the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act is decided. The interim orders
will naturally be subject to the final determination of the case.
With these directions, the Special Leave Petitions stand disposed
of.
6. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we request the
High Court to take up and dispose of Section 34 petition as
expeditiously as possible.

of.

1. After hearing learned counsel for the parties, it appears that
originally Khasra No.1101/966, situated at Gram Panchayat Bajor,
District  Sikar,  was  originally  allotted  to  Government  Higher
Secondary School, Bajor, for use as a school playground. The said
khasra was subsequently re-numbered as 1397/1395, admeasuring 2
hectares. The Rajasthan High Court has dismissed the PIL petition
challenging the cancellation of aforesaid allotment on the premise
that Khasra No.1101/966 was not in dispute. It seems that the fact
1

--- Page 1306 ---
of renumbering of the said khasra was not brought to the notice of
the High Court.
2. In  such  circumstances,  we  dispose  of  the  special  leave
petition at this stage, with liberty to the petitioners:
(i) To file a review petition before the High Court. We request
the High Court to examine the aforesaid aspect and pass an
appropriate order; and
(ii) To raise the aforesaid factual issue in W.P. No. 6171/2026,
which is stated to be pending and in which the cancellation of the
allotment has also been challenged. The petitioners herein, as well
as the writ petitioner in the said case, shall be at liberty to
raise the aforesaid issue therein.
3. With liberty aforementioned, the special leave petition is
disposed of.
4. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

21.08.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras in CRL.
M.P. No.15670 of 2026 in CRL. O.P. No.13619 of 2026. The contention
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO.17001/2026

--- Page 1342 ---
2
of the petitioner is that while granting bail to the petitioner,
the petitioner has been directed to deposit a sum of Rs.10,00,000/-
and such a condition could not have been imposed by the High Court.

of Tamil Nadu has stated before this Court that the matter be
remanded back to the High Court for deciding the same.

passed by the High Court is set aside and the matter is remanded
back to the High Court and the High Court is requested to decide
the matter on merits based upon the material available before the
High Court and no such condition of any deposit be imposed upon the
petitioner.
4. The special leave petition stands disposed of.

               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C) No. 22407/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 22-06-2026
in WP No. 5642/2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Bombay at Aurangabad]
SEVA SAHAKARI SANSTHA M.                           Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
AVADHOOT & ORS.                                    Respondent(s)
(IA No. 185385/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED
JUDGMENT and IA No. 185387/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.)
 
WITH
SLP(C) No. 22420/2026 (IX)
(IA No. 185633/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED
JUDGMENT, IA No. 185639/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T., IA No.
187373/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T. and IA No. 187371/2026 -
PERMISSION TO PLACE ADDITIONAL FACTS AND GROUNDS)
 
Date : 09-09-2026 These matters were called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANOJ MISRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Shivaji M. Jadhav, AOR
                   Mr. Aditya S. Jadhav, Adv.
                   Mr. Brij Kishor Sah, Adv.
                   Ms. Apurva, Adv.
                   Mr. Vignesh Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Dere Kishor Shankar, Adv.
                   Ms. Shivali Chaudhary, Adv.
                   
For Respondent(s) :
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The High Court held the petitioner disqualified to cast his
vote in the election of Committee of management of Nanded District
Central Co-operative Bank on the ground that by the cut off date
the petitioner had not paid all the interest dues which came to be
paid after the cut off date.

--- Page 1392 ---
2. The provisions of sub-section (10) of Section 27 of the
Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960 (for short, “1960
Act”) disqualifies a defaulter member from being a voter.
3. Whether to be considered a defaulter, a service of notice of
demand is necessary or not needs to be examined.  Further, how a
defaulter has been defined under the 1960 Act or the Rules made
thereunder also need to be examined.
4. In view of the above, we deem it appropriate to adjourn the
matter for four weeks so as to enable the learned counsel for the
petitioner to examine the relevant provisions of the Act as well as
the Rules for the purposes of addressing us as to when a member
would be considered a defaulter.
5. As it appears that pursuant to the interim order passed by
this Court, the petitioner has participated in the election.  We
deem it appropriate to require the petitioner to seek instructions

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. A coordinate Bench of this Court (cor. Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and
Alok Aradhe, JJ.) by an order dated 10 th April, 2026 passed in SLP (Crl.)
Nos.19025-19027/2025 has referred the following issue to a larger Bench for
decision:-
“6. In view of the above, we refer the question relating to the
interplay between Rule 311(3) of the Rajasthan High Court
Rules, 1952 and the inherent power under Section 482 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure, coupled with the correctness of the
decision taken in the case of Vivek Rai (Supra), to a larger
1

--- Page 1402 ---
Bench. 
7. The registry is directed to place our order along with the
paper books before the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India for passing
appropriate orders for constitution of the Bench.”
2. We are of the considered opinion that in addition thereto, the reference
may also include interpretation of Rule 48 of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh
Rules, 2008. We, therefore, frame two additional questions as follows:-
(i) Whether in view of Rule 48 of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh
Rules,  2008,  which  have  not  yet  been  struck  down  as
unconstitutional, whether the inherent power under Section 482
can be exercised to grant suspension of sentence?
(ii)  In view of the discordant notes struck in various decisions of
this Court, which of the two decisions - Vivek Rai & Anr. Vs. High
Court of Jharkhand 1 or Daulat Singh Vs. State of Madhya
Pradesh2 lays down correct law?
3. Insofar as the present case is concerned, we grant the petitioner
exemption from surrender for eight weeks with liberty to him to seek extension
thereof on notice to the respondents.
4. The application for suspension of sentence filed by the petitioner, pending
before the High Court, may be decided within such period (eight weeks). The
High Court may proceed to give its decision on such application immediately
upon being notified of this order by the Registry of this Court without waiting for
the petitioner to mention/take steps for enlistment.
5. List the special leave petitions after twelve weeks.

                             O R D E R
Leave granted.
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State.
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that
accused No.2, whose appeal is also pending before this
Court,  had  been  granted  the  relief  of  bail  pending

--- Page 1802 ---
consideration of his appeal by this Court vide order dated
29.07.2025 in Crl.A.NO.3253 of 2025 {SLP (Crl.) No.6884 of
2025};  that  insofar  as  accused  No.1  is  concerned,  a
similar order may be made as he has now completed nine
years’ of incarceration.
Learned counsel for the respondent however objected
to the release of the appellant-accused No.1 herein.
We have perused the order dated 29.07.2025. 
Having regard to the said order and bearing in mind
the fact that the appellant has now completed nine years’
of incarceration and as this is a case of circumstantial
evidence, we find that the relief of bail ought to be
granted to the appellant-accused No.1 also. 
In the circumstances, we direct the said appellant
to be produced before the concerned Sessions Court as
early as possible and the appellant shall be released on
bail subject to the terms and conditions the Sessions
Court may deem appropriate to impose.
